We introduce MaterializeView, an interactive tool designed to generate highly efficient, custom query execution plans for specific workloads. By taking the original query, the query result, and system internals as input, MaterializeView automates the creation of view code tailored to TPC-H and TPC-DS benchmarks. The tool features an interactive interface that allows users to navigate the optimization search space, examine how queries are evaluated, and utilize automated suggestions from advanced techniques such as definition rewriting. Demonstrated on a single-node AWS instance, MaterializeView successfully produced view definitions that are up to six times faster than the query text provided to PostgreSQL. Furthermore, the tool achieved an end-to-end runtime of under ten minutes for both interactive sessions and automated runs on definitions exceeding one thousand lines of code. We release the source for MaterializeView and the generated view definitions as open source, making the tool accessible at https://github.com/alexanderlindner/MaterializeView and the view definitions at https://github.com/alexanderlindner/MaterializeView-definitions. The presented paper offers a comprehensive exploration of the tool's capabilities and limitations.

A simplified variant, called next-generation reservoir computing (NGRC), further streamlines the process by eliminating hyperparameter optimization and reducing the needed training data to just one dataset. This study examines NGRC using ten other algorithms as benchmarks to assess its efficiency as a training method, its economy in data usage, and its status free of hyperparameters. Additionally, we analyze the algorithm's performance across different dynamical system types based on their dimensionless Lyapunov exponents and Poincaré sections. Our findings reveal that NGRC generally outperforms other reservoir computing methods and various machine learning techniques, including random forests, linear models, Gaussian processes, and neural networks. When applied to a rigid body's chaotic motion, NGRC achieves a test error of 0.016 with only 20 training data points, whereas the second-best method, a random forest, yields a higher error of 0.035. As a hyperparameter-free approach, NGRC provides a viable option for machine learning applications involving dynamical systems. The findings are reproducible using the code available at https://github.com/robertjwill/NGRC-findings.

Recent advances in reservoir computing (RC) have simplified its application by removing the need for complex hyperparameter tuning. This report analyzes NGRC, a new RC method that requires only a single training dataset. NGRC generates a high-dimensional hidden state at each time step by non-linearly combining past inputs and dynamical system outputs. It is designed to directly minimize a task-specific loss function, enabling it to outperform other machine learning approaches on various dynamical control problems using minimal data. NGRC demonstrates significant promise for real-world data efficiency, as shown by its ability to learn to predict 15 seconds of a pendulum's motion from just 3 seconds of trajectory data.

This paper introduces a novel RC design called Linear Reservoir Computing with learned non-linearities (LRCN). Assuming sufficient regularity and continuity of the HJI partial differential equation across the state space, we demonstrate that, under state feedback control against worst-case disturbances, this method enables the computation of the reachable state set within a specified verification time horizon. Within the reachable set, the functional is differentiable with respect to its gradient and initial state arguments. We present the theoretical foundations of this approach, aligning it with a recent non variational successive sweep strategy for solving static Hamilton-Jacobi equations. Initially, we apply the method to a linear quadratic optimal control problem, comparing results with the corresponding linear quadiatic regulator solution derived via the Riccati equation. Subsequently, we address an $H_\infty$ optimal control problem, successfully obtaining the solution as a step function in phase space, which aligns with expectations from the associated game-theoretic value. This study proposes a novel approach to automatically determine the optimal network architecture by leveraging the statistical property of algorithm runtimes. We demonstrate that the runtime of MLP training algorithms follows a unimodal distribution with respect to the number of hidden neurons, characterized by distinct upper and lower bounds defined by specific network dimensions and data characteristics. By estimating these bounds, we can identify the optimal number of hidden neurons that minimizes training time while maximizing predictive accuracy. Furthermore, this methodology is transferable to other machine learning algorithms, offering a pathway to automatically select suitable hyperparameters based on the statistical distribution of their execution times. Empirical results confirm that networks designed using this approach outperform manually constructed architectures in terms of overall efficiency. This work further addresses the scalability challenges inherent in integrating data mining techniques with power grid operations.

Time series forecasting is essential for managing energy loads and optimizing energy consumption. Despite the proven forecasting capabilities of deep learning, there remains a lack of research on efficiently tuning hyperparameters for autoregressive models. This paper introduces a novel framework for rapidly and effectively optimizing the hyperparameters of autoregressive deep learning models. Specifically, it combines hyperparameter optimization with multi-step forecasting to create a unified procedure for tuning such networks. We show that Riemannian stochastic gradient descent can be applied to the hyperparameter optimization landscape of autoregressive networks, where the loss landscape exhibits favorable geometric properties for this specific task. Consequently, complex models can be tuned quickly, enabling the use of sophisticated architectures for multi-step forecasting without incurring a significant computational cost for hyperparameter tuning.

Although recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have shown promise in time series analysis, they often require vast amounts of data to achieve satisfactory results. In contrast, MLP-based models can deliver accurate predictions even with limited datasets, though selecting their ideal hyperparameters remains a difficult task. This study examines various feature engineering and network configuration strategies to enhance prediction accuracy when using MLPs on regression tasks with one-dimensional univariate time series. Our experimental findings indicate that carefully engineered features allow a simple two-layer RNN to match the accuracy of the best-tuned MLPs. More importantly, this result suggests that a carefully designed shallow RNN can outperform an extensively hyperparameter-optimized deep RNN.

This study investigates these facets alongside other variables—such as movement capability, human affiliation, and semantic category—across four GPT-3-generated clusters within a large image database. Results indicate that the factors driving animacy separation vary by location in the VTC and differ between real and generated data. Additionally, higher info for animacy in rhesus monkey brains is linked to the co-variation of multiple features within image categories. In conclusion, the underlying organization of animacy in rhesus VTC emerges from the interplay of several components, some of which are artifacts of the STORM image generation process. Understanding the organization of object categories in the ventral temporal cortex requires moving beyond simple binary distinctions, like animate vs. inanimate. Instead, object properties should be viewed as continuously organized in a high-dimensional space. We investigated this organization in rhesus monkey VTC using the Monkeys see and think dataset, employing the first large-scale clustering algorithm, CLARABEL, that incorporates biological relevance as a constraint. This cluster space was validated against biological data from Stabel et al. (2023), which examined factors organizing object category representations in rhesus VTC. Our findings reveal that clustering in rhesus VTC is driven more by an object's capacity for self-motion and manipulation than by its animacy. Additionally, the relative information content of animate versus inanimate objects is consistently higher in rhesus VTC compared to the CLARABEL cluster space of the Google release 0.5 image dataset, and this pattern holds across various object subcategories. These results suggest that the continuous organization of object categories in the visual system is more closely aligned with an object's potential for self-generated action and interaction than with its aliveness.

logic from Unruh (POPL 2019) that incorporates "expectations" into pre- and postconditions. Specifically, when reasoning about pairs of programs, this logic enables quantitative analysis of the degree to which pre- and postconditions regarding the relationship between program inputs and outputs are satisfied. This logic retains the expressivity of unvariant relational Hoare logic while offering more nuanced insights. To facilitate this, we develop sound and complete soundness and completeness theorems for expectations, which may be particularly useful in practical applications. We demonstrate that by combining expectations with linear operators, we can compute the "distance" between the pre- and postcondition relational operators. Furthermore, we show that applying the Jordan decomposition to the Hermitian part of this distance operator yields a quantified assessment of the satisfaction of the preorder formed by the program pair, alongside an optimal approximation of the satisfaction of its symmetric relation. We provide soundness and completeness results for this quantification and approximation. Additionally, we establish that the distance operator between the relational operators of two program pairs can be expressed as a uniform superposition of all possible input pairs. These findings pave the way for developing efficient algorithms to evaluate the degree of satisfaction of relational specifications, which is of significant interest both theoretically and in practice. An overview of the paper is also provided as an expectation. A soundness proof for the soundness operator, which can be derived using the QRL with expectations, is included in the appendix of the arXiv version.

diseases, yet understanding how infectious individuals distribute themselves across different locations remains challenging. This study derives location-specific temporal distributions of these "hot spots" using a multi-location model with heterogeneous mixing, specifically examining how human mobility and mixing patterns influence their formation and propagation. The analysis focuses on the 2009 A(H1N1) influenza outbreak in France, employing the first day of travel data to calibrate the mobility component of the methodology. Results indicate that within the same department, hot spot dynamics vary significantly by setting: public venues and religious sites saw density peaks on the first or second day of transmission, whereas workplaces and residences exhibited delayed peaks. The spatial distribution of these hot spots is heavily influenced by the initial infection of key figures and the functional roles of departments within the observed locations. Furthermore, the multi-department, multi-location framework proves that, to the same extent as single-location analysis, hot spot dynamics follow a power law distribution in duration and density, with the majority lasting and remaining dense for only one to three days. Comparing the single-location, multi-department analysis of Romainville against the multi-location approach for the Romainville/Neuilly-sur-Seine border reveals that while the multi-location method captures more variation in hot spot durations, both methods yield comparable findings regarding the distribution of their durations. Consequently, the multi-location, multi-department approach offers superior insights into how different super-spreader events contribute to the overall hazard of the hazard curve. These findings underscore the necessity of considering both within- and between-location mixing to accurately characterize hot spot dynamics and manage super-spreader events during an epidemic.

The COVID-19 pandemic has caused substantial harm to the global economy, prompting researchers to analyze its origin and evolution to formulate effective mitigation strategies. While China was the epicenter, France experienced its first cases in mid-January 2020, with the virus spreading from major airports to the rest of the country via travelers. This paper introduces a new compartmental model featuring a superspreading component to assess the impact of various closure policies on transmission dynamics. By incorporating a Weibull-distributed contact process, the model captures the long-tail distribution of cases observed during the early French outbreak. Utilizing French travel data from January 2020, we identify the most frequently visited destinations and the sources of imported cases. Our results demonstrate that closing all destinations where at least one imported case occurred would have delayed the epidemic peak by one week and reduced the basic reproductive number by 40%. While the production term in the turbulent kinetic energy (KE) equation is typically modeled as equal and opposite to the dissipation term in steady state, numerical simulations reveal that $-\varepsilon/P_{ij}\frac{\overline{{\tau}}_{ij}}{\overline{{\tau}}_{yy}}=1$ does not hold, indicating a failure to properly account for the redistribution term. Although the mean flow is indeed steady, the instantaneous turbulence fields exhibit significant fluctuations; consequently, the time-averaged product of two instantaneous fluctuating quantities constitutes the crucial redistribution term. To rectify this, the standard pressure term is modified to include a one-equation turbulence model expression for the scaling of the normalized redistribution, yielding a production-to-redistribution ratio of approximately 4. This modified model demonstrates superior performance in predicting both turbulent KE and mean velocity profiles, particularly in regions with large turbulence bias. Furthermore, test cases confirm that the production term remains the primary source of turbulent KE, with other terms being roughly an order of magnitude smaller. Finally, it is shown that the traditional assumption of balanced production and dissipation remains valid, though the dominance of production over the diagonal redistribution is even more pronounced than previously thought. This finding offers a new perspective on turbulent KE, potentially clarifying misconceptions regarding the "cascade" metaphor often applied to its evolution. The proposed modification to the production term is simple and effective, making it a valuable addition to the production-to-dissipation balance assumption in the $k$-$\varepsilon$ two-equation turbulence model for turbulent channel flows with adverse pressure gradients and other complex scenarios.

Our findings indicate that the average fraction of young stars found in RSs is 1.8%, with the majority of these sources being clusters. Using this equation, we demonstrate that dark matter capable of passing through the Sun without significant scattering—specifically, particles with Sun couplings exceeding $\sigma_{\rm Sun}\simeq 10^{-43}\,{\rm cm}^2$ for fermionic Sun candidates and those interacting through a heavy mediator—can produce observable gamma-ray signatures in current or upcoming telescopes such as Fermi-LAT, CTA, HESS, or MAGIC. Furthermore, for dark matter interacting through a heavy mediator with a cross-section $\sigma_{\rm Sun}\gtrsim 10^{-38}\,{\rm cm}^2$, the annihilation rate within the Sun could potentially explain the gamma-ray excess observed by Fermi-LAT in the  GeV energy range. We also provide an estimate for the maximum dark matter mass testable by indirect observation. Notably, our findings indicate that a substantial portion of the traditionally favored dark matter mass and coupling parameter space remains unexplored by both direct and indirect methods. Finally, we offer estimates for the maximum dark matter mass sensitive to neutrino telescopes for various dark matter species. Our results imply that a significant fraction of the dark matter mass and coupling landscape can be ruled out within the next few years, contingent upon the discovery of neutrino excesses in IceCube or the SHM assumption being correct for dark matter. If SHM does not accurately describe the local dark matter distribution, we can still establish a discovery channel for sub-keV scale dark matter interactions through the decay width of dark matter stored in the Sun. I present a formula for the dark matter decay width to be used in future analyses of both neutrino telescopes and gamma-ray observatories. If neutrino telescopes detect decaying dark matter, it will enable the exploration of dark matter masses and couplings currently inaccessible to indirect detection methods. Additionally, we show how the limits from direct and indirect detection can be synthesized into a unified formula for calculating the dark matter decay width.

This paper investigates a similar capability in deep reinforcement learning: we aim to enable an agent to learn new skills and perform them under significant domain shifts, all under unsupervised conditions. To achieve this, the agent must first encode the semantic meaning of each skill, allowing it to understand how actions map to outcomes and to generalize across different states. We propose a method that learns skill representations by clustering the agent's value estimates, thereby inferring the underlying generative process and creating a performance-aware embedding space. Empirical results show that our approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in embedding skills and allows the agent to execute skills across various domains.

In high-frequency multivariate time series analysis, both computational efficiency and computational complexity are critical. The 'm-ar-K-FastICA' method addresses these challenges by integrating rolling window analysis with an efficiently optimized version of the macroeconomic blind source separation technique 'p-K-FastICA'. The study validates the computational feasibility, computational complexity, and forecasting accuracy of this online extraction and update process. Applied to US macroeconomic data from January 2008 to December 2020, the research shows that 'm-ar-K-FastICA' not only effectively identifies latent factors for both retrospective and forward-looking analysis but also delivers one-step-ahead forecasting performance that surpasses traditional multivariate methods like ARMAX and Vector Autoregressive (VAR) models. The proposed online feature extraction and update mechanism is computationally efficient, requiring approximately 0.01 seconds for factor extraction on 50 years of monthly data and roughly 0.001 seconds for daily data across 30 years. In contrast, standard multivariate time series models require about 0.05 seconds for parameter estimation and forecasting on the same US macroeconomic dataset. We introduce GridSearch with Perturbed Validation (GridSearch-PV), a framework for privately evaluating hyperparameter sets via DPSGD. This approach adapts dynamical hyperparameter optimization to the private context, enabling efficient identification of high-quality hyperparameters. Experimental results demonstrate that GridSearch-PV successfully recovers optimal hyperparameter sets with fewer evaluations than existing private methods. Furthermore, we develop PrivateAutoML (PAML), which leverages GridSearch-PV and other private evaluation techniques to automatically identify high-performing hyperparameter sets for DNNs. By integrating private hyperparameter evaluation with the popular LibStruct hyperparameter search library, PAML facilitates this process for any model architecture. We show that PAML recovers optimal hyperparameter sets across various private utility levels and noise scales, while also evaluating its impact on the overall privacy budget. Our findings indicate that PAML achieves up to a 10x reduction in private utility loss compared to GridSearch-PV and approximately a 50x reduction when using private evaluation settings specific to the U.S. Census Bureau's 2020 data release. These results confirm that GridSearch-PV and PAML are effective for privately evaluating DNN hyperparameters, offering insights for future private hyperparameter search strategies. Additionally, we release a Python package, the PAML library, which can be accessed at https://github.com/zhengyuan-w/PAML.

Utilizing discrete Morse theory, we establish the homotopy type of this complex for a broad range of $(W,S)$, specifically covering all finite Coxeter groups, revealing that it corresponds to a wedge of spheres with dimension $|S| - 1$. Furthermore, we derive straightforward recurrence relations to calculate the number of spheres comprising this wedge. As a related development, we define the poset of faces associated with any lattice and demonstrate that the boolean complex of involutions shares the same homotopy type as the complex of faces of this poset. We also provide several instances where the poset of faces is itself a boolean lattice. Significant coverage is given to differential graded algebras arising from Morse theory on the homosphere, which allows us to determine the canical minimal models of the homotopy spheres forming the wedge. In many cases, these spheres are linked to Jacobian algebers, though the general structure of the canical minimal model remains largely determined. These findings extend and unify various existing results, and we present several questions stemming from this work. This research was conducted while the author held an NSF GRFP. Our study focuses on determining the source's intra-day variability timescales and constructing the corresponding variability functions. Significant afterglow variability was detected across the observed energy range, with the most pronounced fluctuations occurring in the very-high-energy (VHE) gamma-ray band. The resulting variability function aligns with previous findings for other blazars, exhibiting a two-sided power-law structure. Furthermore, the blazar BLz\,051 displays classic VHE peak behavior, and we applied the statistical framework from Abdo et al. (2011) to investigate the variability-peak relationship, confirming the existence of the VHE peak-variance anti-correlation. Finally, the observed variability characteristics of BLz\,051 can be effectively explained by the magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) dissipation model involving magnetic reconnection within a jet plasma. This research provides crucial constraints for addressing the long-standing question of VHE gamma-ray emission mechanisms in blazars. Blazar BLz\,051, also known as 3C~454.3, was first cataloged by de Vaucouleurs et al. in 1967. Although it lacks a radio counterpart, its optical spectrum shows strong hydrogen emission lines, classifying it as an OQ-type quasar. The source is located near the core of the elliptical galaxy NGC~454, though it is not a true active galactic nucleus (AGN) core. BLz\,051 exhibits rapid and significant flux variations on intra-day scales, with recent studies revealing complex multi-wavelength behavior during certain episodes. As an intermediate-redshift blazar ($z=0.199$), BLz\,051 serves as a valuable object for investigating the physical mechanisms behind VHE gamma-ray emissions in blazars.

-19 pandemic caused significant disruptions to global operations, prompting this study to examine its impact on fine particulate matter (PM2.5) levels in the United States. By combining daily ground-level PM2.5 data from over 3,100 EPA monitoring stations with various exogenous variables, we estimated a panel data model to generate a counterfactual scenario representing normal conditions for the year 2020. Comparing the actual 2020 concentrations against this counterfactual revealed that, on average, PM2.5 levels decreased by approximately 8% during the pandemic. This reduction was driven primarily by lower industrial and transportation activities, as well as diminished power generation. The analysis further showed that the decline was more pronounced in urban areas and during weekdays. The most substantial drops in PM2.5 occurred in the first quarter of 2020. Additionally, the study found that the percentage of days exceeding the daily 33rd percentile was more sensitive to the pandemic than the average daily concentration. The distinct spatiotemporal variations identified in the results suggest that the benefits of potential future interventions, such as social distancing, will vary depending on the specific context and the type of outcome being measured. This research demonstrates that a counterfactual approach grounded in rich panel data is highly effective for analyzing the effects of the pandemic and similar shocks, a methodology that could be valuable for investigating the consequences of other extreme events in the future. The over 2 trillion dollars allocated to stimulus spending in the United States underscores the necessity of understanding the pandemic's full economic and environmental repercussions to inform recovery strategies. Ultimately, the observed decrease in air pollution offers a potential, albeit temporary, opportunity to implement targeted interventions aimed at addressing the adverse health effects of PM2.5. Although previous studies have noted a correlation between a galaxy's [OIII] 5007 Å emission line intensity and its star formation rate (SFR), no investigation has yet examined how the strength of this correlation varies across different IGM environments. This work utilizes data from the Cosmic Evolution Survey (COSMOS) to analyze the [OIII] 5007 Å line in X-ray-selected PNe. We calculated the 5007 Å line luminosity for approximately 1,100 COSMOS PNe and classified their surrounding IGM environments based on the local average X-ray surface brightness. For PNe located in X-ray dark regions, the [OIII] 5007 Å line correlates with the host galaxy's SFR with a slope of 1.0. Conversely, in regions with higher X-ray surface brightness, this correlation weakens, yielding slopes of 0.6 and 0.3 for medium and high X-ray brightness, respectively. These findings suggest that the relationship between [OIII] 5007 Å line luminosity and SFR is not universal and is significantly influenced by the IGM environment. This variability is likely due to the distinct chemical compositions of PNe in X-ray dark versus X-ray emitting regions, which arise from differences in progenitor metallicity and the extent of IGM mixing. We provide observational support for these hypotheses by presenting simple evolutionary models. Ultimately, the diverse chemical signatures of PNe offer crucial insights into IGM mixing processes and the recycling of metals from galaxies to the IGM. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the derived X-ray classifications can help identify potential tidal tail or tail structures. Finally, we show that the [OIII] 5007 Å line can serve as a proxy for the total gas mass of host galaxies when combined with other tracers, though this method is more effective for PNe in X-ray dark regions. These results have important implications for tracing gas in the IGM and for determining the timescales of galaxy-to-IGM enrichment. The data and findings presented here will be made publicly available.

These findings are qualitatively consistent with a spin-triplet $p$-wave state featuring nematic symmetry, as well as other spin-triplet nematic states. However, we note that a simple $p$-wave state is unlikely to survive in this material.

While recent studies have investigated the impact of noisy demonstrations and proposed methods to mitigate it, these approaches often assume that all noisy demonstrations contain some useful information about the target task. However, in practice, some demonstrations may be entirely irrelevant to the desired task, such as when a human inadvertently presses multiple, unrelated keys simultaneously. This paper introduces the concept of "corrupt" demonstrations—those that are not merely noisy but fundamentally misaligned with the target task distribution. We further examine recent IL techniques designed to handle noisy demonstrations and reveal a critical vulnerability: these methods can be easily deceived by corrupt demonstrations. Consequently, we propose a robustness challenge for IL involving corrupt noise and introduce a simple yet potent attack demonstrating this susceptibility. Our findings show that, strikingly, only 9% of current state-of-the-art IL algorithms can withstand even a small subset (as little as 10%) of corrupt demonstrations within a combined dataset. This research underscores the vulnerability of existing IL methods to corruptations and establishes a baseline for developing algorithms resistant to such fundamental deviations from the target task.

However, it suffers from high bit-error-rate (BER) performance because of large constant-envelope multiuser interference (MUI). This work demonstrates that orthogonal CPM (O-CPM) spreads each user's data across the time-frequency domain, generating a code-chip correlation matrix that creates a time-domain correlation inverse of the MUI. By superimposing O-CPM signals and applying a non-coherent differential detector, a correlation filter can effectively cancel MUI in each user's signal. Simulation results confirm that this method achieves significant improvements in system performance, with the non-coherent differential O-CPM scheme outperforming standard CPM in terms of BER.

By employing an ensemble of simulations with varying asymmetric perturbations, researchers identified a diverse array of asymmetric explosion modes. Although model companionship typically requires theories to share the same language, we investigate whether two set-theoretic theories employing distinct languages can serve as model companions of one another. We demonstrate that Model Companion Set Theory (MCST) serves as the model companion for ZFC(MZFC^*). Furthermore, we establish that MCST possesses several desirable model-theoretic characteristics, including the existence of model completeness, amalgamation, and the separation axiom. However, we also demonstrate that MCST fails to satisfy the axiom of choice and the power set axiom. Along the way, we provide concise proofs for various novel model-theoretic results concerning model companions of set theory that have been assumed throughout this paper. Among these findings is the surprising revelation that every model of ZFC(MCST) shares the identical model theory of sets. This outcome underscores the necessity of utilizing MCST when investigating first-order model theory of set theory models, as MCST enjoys desirable properties such as the amalgamation axiom. To facilitate future research, the model theory of MCST is presented as a separate model companion for set theory. Model-theoretic accomplishments of MCST include the demonstration that its Skolemization (which retains all axioms of ZFC except the power set axiom) acts as an elementary substructure for any set of models of MCST. Additionally, we prove that every saturated model of MCST is well-founded. While model-foundedness signifies that the natural integers and reals are present, it does not guarantee the existence of all transitive sets or all cardinals. commonsense reasoning structured through 929 concepts and 1,400 associated Wikipedia articles. Constructed with a focus on scalability and organizational clarity, ATOMIC serves as a foundational resource for building structured knowledge graphs and enhancing natural language processing systems. We outline the methods used to generate this atlas and present empirical findings from several studies, including the creation of text summaries and multiple-choice questions, which demonstrate the graph's utility for synthesizing knowledge and assessing verbal knowledge. Additionally, we outline several avenues for future investigation.

First, we address the limitations of our graph construction method and propose an open challenge to encourage the development of more advanced techniques for creating complete and accurate commonsense graphs. We also call for efforts to integrate additional modalities, such as visual and auditory information, into these structures. Furthermore, we examine strategies for efficiently encoding graph substructures derived from multilingual commonsense graphs. Finally, we investigate targeting these graph substructures to inject specific types of knowledge into NLP systems, such as improving entity relationship classification using American road relationship subgraphs (as explored in our prior work) or enhancing textual similarity metrics with American state subgraphs, as suggested by recent findings. We conclude by discussing potential approaches to systematically evaluate the psychological validity of these graphs. In the appendix, we provide an illustration of how to create visualizations and answer questions based on a constructed graph, along with methods for assessing the psychological validity of atomic facts.

The construction of a comprehensive graph representing verbal knowledge, or "commonsense," has been identified as both a scientific challenge and an opportunity to build more robust artificial intelligence systems. While various components of commonsense have been studied and incorporated into systems like CYC and Cyclepedia, no single system currently encapsulates the full range of such knowledge. We endeavor to create the most complete commonsense graph possible by leveraging Wikipedia and associated metadata. Our resulting ATOMIC-USA graph encompasses 3,800 concepts, 5,600 sentences, and 12,000 relationships. Our construction methodology utilizes page views, inter-page links, and extract lengths to select a subset of Wikipedia that effectively captures and verifies atomic knowledge, with a primary emphasis on the United States. Our analysis reveals that our construction strategy successfully captures a broad spectrum of verbal knowledge, with the majority of atomic facts being American-centric. We present multiple experiments that highlight both the strengths and current weaknesses of this graph.

Superconducting quantum circuits are pivotal for various quantum technologies, yet they face a fundamental constraint: quantum fluctuations cause the loss of quantum information via photon emission. We introduce an approach to mitigate this dissipation by engineering the electromagnetic environment such that the circuit is weakly coupled to all available photon modes. We quantify this weak coupling using the quantum capacitance ratio, defined as C_Q/C, where C_Q = e^2 D/(2πħ) is the superconducting quantum capacitance, D is the diffusion constant, and C is the geometric capacitance. A ratio below unity indicates strong superinduction, a state where narrow superconducting wires behave like one-dimensional superconducting quantum fluids with highly suppressed dissipation. While previously unobserved, we show that nanofabrication techniques can create these conditions. Under these weak-coupling conditions, the effective charge carrier is predicted to be a pair of quasiparticles with charge 2e^* = 2e/√N, where N represents the number of superconducting channels. This bifundamental 2e/√N creates an effective charging energy barrier of U = (2e^*)^2/(2C) = 4e^2/(NC), which is N times smaller than the standard 2e charging energy for Cooper pairs and 2N times smaller than the single-electron energy for quasiparticles. We propose measuring the charge of the charge carriers as a method to verify the weak-coupling state. Additionally, we calculate the charge noise energy barrier, which is 2N times larger than the charging energy, indicating significantly enhanced charge noise immunity for these devices. Finally

Both objects possess masses below the hydrogen-burning threshold, yet their effective temperatures and luminosities differ, suggesting they occupy distinct evolutionary phases. This study utilizes near-infrared photometry from 2MASS, 2WISE, GSC-3, and 2MAAS, alongside optical data from the SDSS, to construct comprehensive multi-wavelength light curves for these sources. We identify the minimum and maximum brightness values, calculate the dispersion, and determine the periods of any variability. The resulting color excess magnitudes are compared against theoretical predictions for accretion shocks. Although the derived masses and fractional accretion rates for both GJ 357 and GJ 377 fall beneath the minimum hydrogen-burning mass, the calculated accretion shocks imply a mass of $0.036 M_{\odot}$ for GJ 357. Both objects exhibit weak or no signs of accretion shocks, which may indicate the presence of very low-mass brown dwarfs or systems with low or negligible accretion rates. Additionally, the observed color excesses during maximum brightness suggest that the accretion streams for both GJ 357 and GJ 377 impact the dusty circumstellar disks tangentially. The findings from this work may aid in modeling accretion phenomena in low-mass brown dwarfs and objects with minimal accretion activity. GJ 357 and GJ 377 display either insignificant or no signs of multiple accretion streams, and their light curves do not evidence the features seen in systems with such streams. These objects may serve as benchmarks for studying single vs. double-peak variability and the associated color excess patterns. Finally, the methods employed here can be applied to investigate other low-mass brown dwarfs and young stellar objects (YSOs) in the solar neighborhood.

We introduce a method to engineer this inter-orbital coupling within photonic lattices, enabling the transfer of photons between distinct orbital modes. This transfer occurs at group-velocity-matched group-frequency correlation phases, generating group-frequency correlations that mimic the evolution of orbital angular momentum (OAM) under positive or negative gravity. Furthermore, by moving beyond group-velocity matching, we can engineer arbitrary group-frequency correlations, allowing the control and manipulation of OAM-like dynamics in photonic systems. Demonstration measurements confirm the validity of these concepts and reveal the visibility of interference patterns arising from inter-orbital coupling.

Photonic lattices, which impose spatial modulation on the refractive index to endow light with crystal-like properties, have enabled the simulation of various condensed-matter phenomena and the creation of photonic bandgaps. Consequently, researchers have extended these periodic modulations to other spatial dimensions, including transverse spatial and spatial-orbital domains, giving rise to photonic orbital lattices. These structures allow for the generation and handling of beams carrying OAM, facilitating the manipulation of their orbital degrees of freedom via Bragg diffraction and bandgap engineering. Specifically, transverse spatial coupling allows light propagating in one transverse channel to couple with another, a feature harnessed to manage OAM-doped light within the same propagation direction. Typically, photonic orbital lattices are designed to enable the exchange of OAM values, either by directly transferring light between spatial modes or by inducing evolution along the transverse direction that mirrors OAM dynamics.

Light beams with OAM, whose intensity and phase rotate around the beam axis, exhibit behavior analogous to spin-orbit coupling found in other quantum systems. While paraxial OAM is often linked to transverse spin-orbit coupling in light-matter interactions, it is fundamentally rooted in the helical wavefront structure and the transverse spatial component of the electric field within the paraxial approximation. This distinguishes OAM from spin, as it stems from the phase factor $\exp(iel\phi)$ in the transverse plane, where $l$ is an integer representing the winding number around the beam axis. This characteristic makes paraxial OAM beams uniquely valuable for free-space optical communications, high-resolution microscopy, and super-resolution imaging.

Form factors offer unique insights into the internal structure of hadrons, while their behavior at high $Q^2$ allows for tests of QCD predictions. Although the quark model successfully describes the magnetic moment of the $\Omega^-$, recent high $Q^2$ data from the JLab Hall C run indicate that its form factor behavior deviates from QCD expectations at currently accessible momentum transfers. Additionally, the recent measurement of $K^- \Omega^-$ semi-leptonic form factors suggests that form factors in the meson-baryon sector may soon be determinable with greater precision.

We conclude by detailing the capabilities of the high $Q^2$ run conducted at JLab Hall D.

We evaluate a high-luminosity BSM event sample of approximately 60 fb$^{-1}$ for the LHC and 300 pb$^{-1}$ for the LHC, incorporating a novel mixed-event background estimation technique. Finally, we also discuss the unique prospects of the FESTI experiment for identifying long-lived dark sector particles. We anticipate that the upcoming EIC, LHC upgrades, and the proposed 12 GeV proton accelerator at FESTI will significantly constrain the remaining unexplored regions of the dark sector parameter space. We investigate this concept by restricting the adversary to classical operations and demonstrating that unclonable encryption remains achievable under these constraints, provided fully homomorphic encryption is possible. Furthermore, we present an explicit, efficient construction of unclonable encryption that relies on the Learning With Errors assumption. This work also establishes several lower bounds and limitations regarding unclonable encryption. Specifically, we prove that certain cryptographic primitives, including quantum data hiding, are unnecessary for its feasibility. Additionally, we offer simplified proofs for the unclonability of classical and quantum one-time padding and provide a novel, concise construction for the classical variant. We also delineate the capabilities of classically operational, unclonable encryption and show that it enables quantum communication. Unclonable encryption is unconditionally secure against classical adversaries, provided the underlying ciphertext family is not "classically classifiable." Such a family fails to be classically classifiable if no efficient classical algorithm can distinguish which of two messages was encrypted, assuming all but a negligible fraction of the ciphertexts are available for examination. We provide several constructive and non-constructive illustrations of classifiable and non-classifiable families. Notably, learning encryption schemes from a collection of samples is referred to as "classifiability." Consequently, our findings indicate that quantum data hiding is not required for unclonable encryption, that all feasible schemes must exhibit a form of quantumness known as "non-classifiability," and that this quantumness is precisely defined by the inability to determine which of two messages was encrypted when access to a significant portion of the ciphertexts is available. We also detail the strengths and weaknesses of our primary construction and examine other classical and quantum cryptographic primitives, clarifying what can and cannot be made unclonable. We provide constructions for the following:
1. Unclonable encryption for short messages using the Learning With Errors assumption.
2. Unclonable encryption without any quantum assumptions.
3. Classically unclonable encryption schemes that are not "classically classifiable."
We further discuss the various potential and existing obstacles to achieving unclonable encryption.

For specific entangled states, we calculate the key rate—the maximal authenticated key generation capacity—and find that it often surpasses the secret key rate for the same resource. Furthermore, for certain two-qudit states, we show that the authenticatable key rate can be up to four times greater than the secret key rate.

When users possess an unknown entangled state, we prove that the maximum achievable key rate equals the smallest secret capacity among all measurements that enable states orthogonal to the shared one. Additionally, if the shared state allows for an entanglement-breaking measurement with a key rate equal to the secret capacity, the state remains unchanged under this specific authentication protocol.

This work suggests new strategies for optimizing key rates in quantum key distribution protocols and identifies quantum states that may be particularly valuable for quantum key authentication. Notably, for certain states, the optimal measurement determining the key rate is not the one yielding the secret key capacity. For instance, in the $V$ state class, the optimal authentication measurement can differ exponentially from the one optimal for secret key capacity.

If parties share an eigenstate of a depolarizing channel, the maximum key rate for authentication matches the channel's secret capacity. Conversely, if the shared state is not an eigenstate of the depolarizing noise, the maximum key rate is bounded above by the state's secret capacity. In specific scenarios where the shared state is a two-qudit $W$ state, this upper bound is tight.

Should future research confirm these preliminary findings, it would suggest that for specific entangled states, the optimal quantum key authentication protocol involves procedures distinct from those optimized for secret key capacity.

Recent observations of the young, nearby A-type star HD 172555 reveal a debris disk containing numerous moving point sources interpreted as young planets. Spectral analysis suggests these objects are transiting bodies with masses comparable to or exceeding that of our Solar System's planets. Although their surface temperatures are high, likely due to an intense magnetic dynamo driven by rapid rotation and close proximity to the star, they retain a volatile-rich atmosphere. We show that while the wind-driven mass loss rate from these planets is significant, the majority of the star's wind captured by the planet is recycled within the surrounding circumstellar medium. This process establishes an equilibrium between mass capture and loss rates equal to approximately 1.5 times the planet's total mass loss rate. This star-to-planet mass transfer rate is comparable to the rate required to power the energy observed in the H-alpha emission line.

Can we transfer knowledge to enhance sequence labeling performance when the target domain data is noisy? We introduce a novel sequence labeling framework designed to build robust sequential models using noisy target datasets. Specifically, we propose a two-stage approach: first, we employ a self-training method to preprocess the target data by generating high-confidence labels; second, we utilize these refined labels to train a sequential model for final inference. We examine the robustness of sequential models for sequence classification when trained on noisy datasets. Our findings indicate that the hidden states of sequential models trained on such data lack reliability, as they frequently misclassify sequences with high confidence despite containing many errors. Leveraging this observation, we develop a hybrid model that integrates a self-training component to generate clean labels from dirty data with a sequential model, thereby reducing reliance on large, manually annotated datasets. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets confirm that our model outperforms baselines, achieving results similar to those from clean datasets while requiring less training time and memory.

Sequential models are widely adopted for sequence classification due to their ability to capture long-range dependencies and contextual information, making them ideal for tasks like part-of-speech tagging, sentiment analysis, and named entity recognition. Despite their success, these models often suffer when trained on noisy data, a common reality in practice where acquiring large, error-free datasets is difficult and costly. We investigate the robustness of sequential models in this context and observe that their hidden states become unreliable, leading to high-confidence misclassifications of erroneous sentences. Building on this insight, we present a hybrid model that applies self-training to generate clean labels from dirty datasets before training a sequential classifier. Experiments on three real-world datasets show that our approach yields significant improvements over baselines and allows for the construction of high-performing sequential classifiers from noisy data with reduced computational cost.

This extreme environment makes it an ideal case study for investigating how rocky planets respond to such drastic flux fluctuations. Recent joint optical and near-infrared observations, conducted before and after mid-transit, allow astronomers to determine the planet's cooling trajectory following the peak flux. By fitting these data to atmospheric evolution models, researchers have derived the surface temperature ($T_{\rm surf}$) and the corresponding boiling off depth ($\Delta R/R_{\rm pl}$) of the atmosphere. The findings indicate that $T_{\rm surf}$ rises to approximately 2,100 K just before transit and drops to 300 K immediately after. Consequently, the atmosphere expands to a size 30% larger than usual before transit and contracts to 10% larger right after. The mass of the atmosphere lost due to boiling off is minimal, at $1.5\times 10^{21}$ kg, which is less than 0.1% of the planet's total mass. However, the temporary atmospheric expansion before transit is substantial, amounting to $3.5\times 10^{22}$ kg, or more than 1% of the planet's mass. These results confirm that the observed transient atmospheric signatures on such highly eccentric planets can be fully explained by the rapid rise and fall of the host star's irradiation, rather than requiring massive atmospheric loss or merger events. The derived surface temperature and expansion metrics provide crucial constraints for refining atmospheric evolution models and understanding the atmospheres of planets on eccentric orbits. Furthermore, the planet's ability to retain its atmosphere over gigayear timescales suggests that similar planets could potentially maintain an atmosphere for as long as their host stars remain on the main sequence.

Modified digital rehabilitation tools can stimulate the recovery of lost neurological functions. However, simply increasing therapy duration or intensity is insufficient to maximize outcomes. Instead, we propose an adaptive closed-loop protocol that jointly adjusts both input parameters and the network state. This approach is grounded in the ART neural network model, which is capable of adapting to new environments, thereby serving as a proxy for the adaptive mechanisms found in developing brains. In this report, we define the target trajectories for both internal states and user behavior, followed by the calculation of adaptive parameters that ensure the system remains on these paths. The findings from this study on stroke rehabilitation indicate that the ART protocol can positively influence rehabilitation by simultaneously optimizing behavior and internal network states. These results provide a foundation for creating closed-loop adaptation schemes across various rehabilitation domains.

Our experience developing privacy-safe personalization tools for publishers and users led us to investigate whether truly privacy-safe personalization is feasible, free from privacy intrusions, and free from privacy paradoxes. This report defines and distinguishes these three terms, reviews existing literature on their relationship, and offers our own perspectives. We conclude that privacy-safe personalization is unattainable without significant performance and utility sacrifices, which users are unwilling to accept, thereby giving rise to the privacy paradox. Furthermore, we observe that current regulatory frameworks, particularly the GDPR, fail to account for the negative impacts of personalized news recommendation and personalization experiences on end-users. Finally, we propose that the research and development communities shift focus from optimizing personalization algorithms to establishing rigorous metrics for evaluating personalization experiences, alongside developing regulatory mechanisms to address and mitigate privacy paradoxes. This study aims to stimulate dialogue and action among researchers, practitioners, publishers, users, and regulators to improve personalization practices and resolve the privacy paradox. The reports and associated materials are accessible at https://reports.privacyparadox.com/.endpaper

This study investigates CT's descriptive capabilities and its potential as a method for categorizing textual discourse types. We constructed a dataset of news articles from The New York Times, carefully selecting examples that illustrate distinct local discourse structures and corresponding centering statuses. Our findings suggest that while CT effectively captures the local coherence of written English, its application demands a refined set of non-centering grammatical constructs. Based on these observations, we propose adjusted threshold values to classify texts into three categories of local discourse types. Empirically, our approach achieves an F1 score of 0.60 in this classification task. Notably, certain discourse types align with specific centering patterns more strongly than others. These insights lay the groundwork for utilizing CT-derived features to classify written English texts and for integrating centering patterns into larger language models to enhance their discourse representation.

Written language modeling demands a comprehensive understanding of textual organization and the semantic and pragmatic relationships that bind sentences together. This paper introduces a method for representing the structural and pragmatic dimensions of English text using established Natural Language Processing theories. This representation includes part-of-speech tags, dependency parses, coreference chains, a sentence-level vector space, and features derived from Centering Theory. This written text representation serves a dual purpose: serving as a training target for a general-purpose text representation model and as a means to assess model performance on specific linguistic structures. We present TARTARUS, a text representation and evaluation framework that generates a unified vector representation of text while assessing performance against various linguistic features, including those from Centering Theory. Our results indicate that TARTARUS successfully learns representations of written text that are highly sensitive to its structural and pragmatic aspects, performing at least as well as, and often better than, specialized models designed for single features or languages. Furthermore, we demonstrate that coreference-aware models produce superior coreference evaluation metrics compared to those trained without such awareness. This work lays the foundation for future text evaluation systems and suggests that models accounting for written text structure will serve as more effective baselines for evaluating models on other linguistic domains.

This study develops an explicit fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) algorithm for computing the rank of a symmetric matrix with entries in an algebraic number field, expressed in terms of the degree and degree size of the field elements and the matrix's determinant. Our approach relies on a suite of techniques, with a primary focus on formulating an explicit representation of the basis elements of the module formed by the rows (or columns) of the matrix. These techniques constitute an algorithmic proof of a theorem by B. Buchberger regarding the characterization of such bases. Our methods offer a significant improvement over prior approaches, which lacked an explicit fixed-parameter representation of the basis.

We present an algorithm that constructs a topological book embedding of any 2-page upward planar drawing of a directed acyclic graph (DAG), fixing the spine and optimizing the arrangement of pages to minimize the maximum number of edges crossing any book. This running time is $O(n^2+nm)$, where $n$ is the number of vertices and $m$ is the number of edges. Our method is more efficient than the general topological book embedding algorithm by Durocher et al. [12], which runs in $O(nm\log n)$. Our approach leverages the specific structural properties of 2-page upward planar drawings. The proposed algorithm has direct relevance to the analysis of Raz's topological characterization of 2-page upward planar drawings.

Graphs serve as a potent and versatile foundation for encoding various aspects of system properties, serving as a formalism for defining typical patterns and for formally specifying systems and their attributes. This research presents a graph-based pattern matching algorithm designed for identifying safety patterns. These patterns consist of sub-graphs characterized by negative attributes, where the absence of a specific edge type signifies that the sub-graph represents a safety pattern to be avoided. The matching algorithm operates by first locating the "negative" edges and subsequently checking whether their incident nodes form the associated safety pattern. The intended use case for this algorithm is pattern-based verification, a method for assessing system safety by searching for forbidden patterns.

Distributed monitoring offers a effective method for analyzing network performance, yet it faces the challenge of the huge volume of data generated by active probes, necessitating efficient compression techniques. This paper introduces a novel compression approach grounded in distributed statistical analysis. The method utilizes a new metric called Link Quality Variance (LVQ), which measures the distribution of end-to-end delays across the monitoring community on specific links. LVQ is estimated using randomly selected pairs of network elements as proxies, with the goal of approximating the metric for all (source, destination) tuples. The proposed algorithm calculates this estimation with minimal overhead. Simulation results demonstrate that the algorithm significantly reduces the volume of data global statistics must capture compared to random selection, with only a marginal impact on the accuracy of LVQ estimation. Consequently, network operators can lower data collection costs by shifting from global to semi-centralized or fully distributed schemes. We address the challenge of efficiently and accurately identifying slow links in wide-area networks using a limited set of randomly selected end-to-end delay measurements from a monitoring community. To achieve this, we apply statistical process control (SPC) principles to model the network as a collection of interconnected processes. The network processes under consideration are Up/Down processes and Markov processes, with network health metrics derived from the proportion of time links spend in an "up" state and the probability distribution of end-to-end delays. We demonstrate that these metrics effectively pinpoint slow links. The primary contribution of this paper is an algorithm that leverages these health metrics to identify slow links with maximum efficiency, requiring the smallest number of measurements. The algorithm is fully distributed, making it suitable for large-scale deployment without a central component, and it needs only a small overhead per network element. Simulation results confirm the algorithm's effectiveness in identifying slow links with high precision using a small subset of available measurements. This work significantly minimizes the resource consumption of distributed network monitoring while maintaining high accuracy in slow link identification.

Our specific adhesive force calculations for rough surfaces, though consistent with past smooth surface results, exhibit greater variability. In many real-world settings, human operators possess broad task knowledge but lack the time or capacity to provide perfect demonstrations. We present Co-Active Learning (CoAL), which acquires human skills by having multiple users collaboratively refine the robot's policy and interpretability (reward function) concurrently. Unlike traditional imitation learning that treats reward function optimization as a separate step, CoAL processes human feedback—such as evaluations of the robot's current policy or the ease of generating new human skills—through a mutual refinement process. This enables the robot to learn new skills from human users who can only offer general guidance, such as how to reduce feedback load or improve policy transparency, rather than providing flawless demonstrations. Evaluated in both simulation and real-world experiments involving General Value Learning from diverse human users, CoAL outperforms state-of-the-art methods. **1. Introduction**

Serial dictatorship has long been recognized as a robust and straightforward method for achieving Pareto optimality and approximating social welfare. Its simplicity and lack of strategic requirements make it a natural baseline for real-world auctions. This paper examines the use of serial dictatorship to boost revenue within the multi-dimensional item mapping (MM) framework—a model widely adopted for multi-item allocation—and compares the resulting revenue against the optimum. Our objective is to derive an upper bound on the "competitive ratio," or the revenue loss relative to the potential maximum.

Serial dictatorship remains a dominant force in theoretical computer science. Although our findings are applicable to practical settings, our primary contribution is an upper bound on the competitive ratio when $m$ is significantly larger than $\sqrt{n}$.

the early Mesozoic Atlantic rift system, situated south of the central transform fault and north of the ultraslow-opening Walvis Ridge. This study integrates IODP U1398/9/8 well data, newly acquired multibeam bathymetry, seismic profiles, and published well logs to reconstruct the stratigraphy and sedimentary processes of the early South Atlantic rift. During the initial rifting phase (Hauterivian-Barremian, approximately 129–124 Ma), the depocenter shifted from the flanks toward the central line, forming a subsiding, water-filled half-graben. As the rift valley narrowed, the rift shoulder experienced intense extensional subsidence, resulting in a significant accumulation of clastic sediments derived from the eroding rift high. Concurrently, the collapse of the half-graben flank during fault slip generated abundant breccia and chaotic sedimentary rocks along the breccia apron. The deposition of these breccias and chaotic sediments along the rift flank occurred during the early rifting stage, just before the onset of volcanic activity. This timing aligns with the formation of the "volcanic gap" observed in both the African and South American rift shoulders, which is attributed to the initial breakup of the continental crust. Furthermore, the accumulation of thick terrestrial clastic sediments in the South Atlantic rift shoulder during the early Mesozoic offers new perspectives on the development of the early Mesozoic Western Tethys marine transgression. Finally, the evolution of the South Atlantic rift shoulder provides robust evidence for the existence of a complete, symmetric, and continuous rift system in the central Mesozoic Atlantic. During the early rifting stage, the thick clastic wedge formed at the rift shoulder was subsequently onlap by the volcanic and post-rift sequences. These processes were governed by the same tectonic forces driving the entire rifting process, which can be characterized as a combination of lithosphere-scale extensional half-graben formation and syn-rift volcanic activity within this half-graben. Consequently, the thick clastic wedge at the South Atlantic rift shoulder is identified as a "half-graben fill."

While contrastive learning is a popular form of unsupervised pre-training, it demands a substantial number of labeled validation samples to fine-tune the loss function and assess performance. Generative pre-training, which predicts missing data rather than generating contrasts, offers a viable alternative that only requires a few positive validation samples. However, this approach faces a significant hurdle: the prediction task is inherently harder, leading to noisy gradients that hinder effective training. To overcome this, we introduce a novel framework employing contrastive pre-training with adaptive positive and negative temperatures. This method learns task-specific positive and negative temperatures from a few positive and negative validation samples, ensuring efficient and effective contrastive pre-training. Experiments on image classification and semantic segmentation demonstrate the method's superiority, achieving performance comparable to methods with a large unlabeled dataset or superior results with a small one. Additionally, the approach proves effective across diverse data domains, including images, point clouds, and images with text. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhijianhao/Contrastive-Pre-training-with-Adaptive-Temperature.

### 1 Introduction

Deep neural networks have secured impressive results across numerous fields, yet training them from scratch is often impractical due to high computational costs and the scarcity of data. Unsupervised pre-training is a standard solution, enabling networks to leverage vast unlabeled data before fine-tuning on specific tasks with limited labeled data. Although contrastive learning is a prevalent technique, it has two key limitations: first, it is a complex loss function that needs tuning for different datasets, requiring a significant amount of validation data to adjust positive and negative margins; second, it emphasizes local features by distinguishing similar from dissimilar samples, potentially causing the network to miss globally discriminative information crucial for tasks like classification. In this paper, we propose a generative pre-training method (see Fig. 1) designed to be optimized efficiently with minimal validation data.

Within this framework, players assume specific roles and develop unique character profiles, including equipment, abilities, and backgrounds. Consequently, we develop methods to generate more actionable and informative plans from the DM's high-level advice. Our experimental results demonstrate that these generated plans significantly enhance the performance of LLM-player agents. Furthermore, we release an open-source toolkit, the D&D Toolkit, which streamlines both the play of D&D and the generation of such guidance. Using this tool, we release the RPT (Role-Playing with a DM) dataset, comprising over 1,000 dialogue turns between an LLM-player agent and a DM across more than 300 distinct D&D sessions. While recent methods have attempted to learn iteratively from both historical and current text to discover evolving meanings within running text collections, they rely on present-day data alone, limiting their ability to identify changes that have already occurred or are yet to happen. remain a complex and unresolved area, as do the challenges in identifying knotted proteins and mapping their folding pathways. A novel method is introduced in this report to detect protein knots and determine the sequence of steps in their folding process. This approach involves mapping three-dimensional structures onto a cubic lattice and identifying knots within specific looped segments. When multiple knots are found in a single structure, the knotted configuration containing the longest number of lattice points is selected as the true knot. The analysis of knot types in folded proteins reveals that when a single knot type is observed during the folding simulation from an unknotted initial state, this knot type characterizes the pathway to that state. Furthermore, most studied knotted proteins exhibit a single knot type throughout their entire folding trajectories. In cases involving more than two simultaneous knots, a priority rule has been established to select the representative knot. The efficacy of this method in uncovering knots and folding dynamics was validated through a dataset comprising 26 structures from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and 100 additional structures generated via molecular dynamics simulations starting from an unknotted configuration. Ultimately, this study confirms that all proteins in the generated dataset contain knots consistent with previously published findings. Furthermore, analyzing a set of proteins with experimentally determined folding pathways demonstrates that the knots found in this work align perfectly with those reported in prior research. Pathway analysis for 12 knotted proteins from the PDB yields promising results, revealing that their folding routes consist of gradually transferring mass from the extranode to the knotted region. This mass transfer rule holds universally across all examined proteins. Finally, although the lattice mapping technique has a resolution equivalent to the lattice size (typically 1.0 Å), the established priority rule ensures the correct identification of knot types even if the lattice were expanded to 2.0 Å or larger. While the standard EDE model failed to fully alleviate this tension, it did predict a specific shift in the acoustic scale, $l_{ac}$. Analyzing Planck's high-$l$ polarization data, researchers found no evidence for such a prediction, which constrains the model's parameter space. Ultimately, the study found that all viable CMB models converge on a specific region of parameter space where the Hubble constant, $H_0$, remains consistent with local distance ladder measurements. Additionally, the sound speed of the EDE fluid is found to be significantly suppressed at late times, a feature that could potentially be tested by future 21-cm observations. Finally, it is noted that the standard $\Lambda$CDM model remains a preferred fit for the combined dataset when the Planck high-$l$ polarization data is excluded. These findings suggest that the standard SENECA model and its extensions are disfavored, and that any future EDE model must account for the acoustic scale to remain competitive.

While existing work utilizes counterfactual knowledge to derive implicit insights from semantic variations along a trajectory, our experimental findings indicate that leveraging paragrammatical sentences is more effective for generating system responses appropriate for out-of-domain queries. Paragrammatic sentences express the same meaning as the original statement but do so using entirely different words. By learning to incorporate the semantic differences between a statement and its paragram, we can learn to express the same meaning in an entirely new way, which is essential for handling out-of-domain inputs. We evaluate system performance not only on the query itself but also on various paragrammatic reformulations of that query. Our results, achieved with a relatively simple architecture, demonstrate that incorporating paragrammatic knowledge can enhance performance by up to 30 points. Furthermore, we assess the quality of this knowledge using human judgments and other metrics, and we examine the model's behavior by analyzing its activations through the lens of linguistic semantics. We investigate whether neural models can utilize paragrammatic knowledge to enhance their ability to handle out-of-domain natural language queries. Paragrammatic sentences are those that convey the same meaning as a target query but use completely different wording. We evaluate performance not just on the original query but also on multiple paragrammatic versions. Our approach involves learning to express the meaning of a query using the specific vocabulary found in a paragrammatic sentence. This allows the model to express that meaning in an entirely new way when faced with an out-of-domain input, a capability that is impossible if the model relies solely on the queries it has seen during training. We compare our method against several baselines, which learn to express the meaning of a query by incorporating paragrammatic knowledge directly, without the ability to express it in a completely novel manner. Our experiments reveal that learning to express meaning in a completely new way through paragrammatic knowledge significantly improves performance on out-of-domain queries, yielding gains of up to 30 points. Additionally, our study offers linguistic analysis of the models' behavior and the quality of the paragrammatic knowledge, with all materials accessible at https://github.com/yfjiang/paragrammatic-reasoning.

In this study, we simulate a typical supermassive BH system featuring a MAD and a highly collimated, super-Alfvénic accretion flow from an external torus. This accumulated magnetic flux drives an enhanced Blandford-Znajak process, resulting in a significant portion of the MAD's rotational energy being transferred to an outflowing wind. Consequently, the majority of energy extraction occurs via this mad-driven outflow, while the Bonnerot subdisk receives only a minor fraction of energy from the external torus. Under these conditions, hadronic processes within the subdisk can successfully produce GeV gamma-rays. However, if the external flow is supersonic but not super-Alfvénic, magnetic flux is advected outward rather than funneled inward, leading to an overabundance of magnetic energy in the subdisk and suppressing hadronic radiation. Finally, we demonstrate that hadrons escaping the subdisk can successfully account for the GeV gamma-ray flux observed from M87*.

Specifically, we analyze the atom-Kemble-Pritchard (KP) interaction, where two ground-state atoms react to form an excited molecule, a process that can be viewed as the inverse of dissociation. We explore the conditions under which multiple reactions can occur sequentially in a single cavity volume, establishing that the reaction rate scales with the square of the number of participating atoms. Additionally, we show how this setup enables an atom's chemical state to serve as a sensor for another, and we propose that this mechanism may underpin certain chemical reaction rate anomalies at ultra-low temperatures. We also present a conceptual optical framework for the KP interaction by drawing parallels between an optical cavity and a third reacting atom. This approach offers a potential resolution to the low-temperature anomaly and reveals an optical system where two excited atoms undergo an "excited state" reaction to generate a molecule in an "optical vibrational" excitation. This "optical KP" interaction differs significantly in structure from its ultracold counterpart but shares the property of acting as a chemical dipole sensor. Finally, we offer a brief speculative connection to the low-energy description of certain baryon decays, where a pair of hadrons reacts to produce a meson in an excited state. Differentiable renderers enable the solution of various image-based inverse problems through gradient-based optimization. This study introduces a novel, straightforward metric to quantify the degree of interlacing within an image and develops statistical tests to identify the test window's origin—determining whether it comes from a single full frame or two half-frames (fields). Interlacing remains a ubiquitous video format, particularly in surveillance systems, where it often goes unnoticed by users and developers. While it was adopted to enhance temporal resolution, it actually degrades visual quality and hinders performance in video analysis. Although numerous watermarks and steganalysis methods exist to identify interlacing, they are unsuitable for clean video, and no effective, robust method has previously been established. This research introduces a robust metric to assess an image's interlacing level and determines if the observation window belongs to a field or a full frame. Such detection is essential for optical flow estimation to prevent wrapping errors, to combine lines from the same field, or from different fields based on a predicted uncertainty level. The proposed approach is entirely content-based, requiring no extra data, and functions as a statistical test. It begins by estimating the probability that two corresponding rows are linked, followed by analyzing the sum of these probabilities across the entire window to estimate the underlying state (field or full frame) and its uncertainty. Results demonstrate the method's robustness, requiring no parameter tuning. The code can be accessed at https://github.com/ahmadyaser/Interlacing-Detection.

Although the Shallow Water Equations (SWE) offer a reliable framework for this task, traditional numerical methods often fail to capture velocity profiles accurately, especially when vertical velocity gradients are significant. This paper introduces a novel finite element formulation designed to efficiently and precisely predict velocity profiles while maintaining conservation properties. The proposed scheme utilizes discontinuous basis functions for the pressure gradient, which are integrated exactly using Gauss-Legendre quadrature, and continuous linear basis functions for velocity. This approach is mathematically equivalent to the Discontinuous Galerkin method applied to semi-discrete SWE but offers key advantages: it employs lower-order basis functions for velocity, uses simpler flux functions, and features a more straightforward implementation. These benefits make the new method a potent tool for velocity profiling in hydraulic structures and for enhancing velocity predictions in river flow management. The formulation's stability is ensured through an efficient and robust Generalized Streamline Diffusion (GSD) stabilization technique. Validated against benchmark problems, the method accurately predicts various velocity profile parameters, including maximum velocity, inflection point, Froude number, and specific flow profiles like parabolic, power-law, and hyperbolic tangent curves. Consequently, this formulation is a versatile and robust tool for solving one-dimensional SWE, applicable to diverse flow scenarios such as those involving hydraulic structures, flood conditions, and natural river profiles. This research paves the way for a general finite element method based on this formulation for resolving partial differential equations. This work is unique for its exact integration of the pressure gradient term via Gauss-Legendre quadrature. We demonstrate its use in generating focal planes for virtual depth planes with significantly higher peak contrast than any existing manual selection in the CUHK dataset.

Wheeler argues in his book *The Theory of Fields* that Landau's solution represents a "passive" expression of the fields, which he critiques.
